section_summaries.epidemiology: HIV has driven the global resurgence of tuberculosis since the 1980s, especially in southern Africa, increasing the risk of active tuberculosis by at least 20-fold. Re-infection, rather than relapse, is a more common cause. HIV infection can disproportionately affect individuals with drug-resistant tuberculosis. HIV may have contributed to an increase in clinical malaria episodes by up to 28% in southern Africa. In areas of stable malaria transmission, HIV-positive pregnant women are more likely to experience clinical malaria, higher parasitemia, anemia, and adverse birth outcomes, particularly with CD4 counts <350 cells/µL. HIV-positive people are at a greatly increased risk of pneumococcal disease, which is more frequent and severe with lower CD4 counts or other comorbidities, and is more common among smokers. Streptococcus pneumoniae is the dominant cause of bacterial meningitis among people with HIV in southern Africa, associated with high mortality.
section_summaries.pathogenesis: HIV infection increases the risk of progressing to active tuberculosis after recent infection and reactivating latent tuberculosis. Tuberculosis can cause immune reconstitution disease (paradoxical or unmasking) in HIV-positive individuals starting antiretroviral therapy. Laboratory studies suggest tuberculosis may accelerate HIV disease progression, increasing mortality risk if antiretroviral treatment is delayed. Placental malaria in HIV-positive pregnant women is associated with increased expression of CCR5, a co-receptor for HIV cell entry, and an increase in maternal viral load. Malarial anemia, particularly in children, has indirectly contributed to HIV transmission via transfusion of unscreened, HIV-infected blood. Transient increases in HIV viral load after malaria episodes have been noted in HIV-positive people not on antiretroviral therapy, though clinical relevance is unclear.
section_summaries.clinical_manifestations: The clinical presentation of tuberculosis is altered in HIV-positive people, often appearing atypical and more subtle. Pulmonary tuberculosis is less likely to involve upper lobe disease or cavitation, especially with advanced immunosuppression, and may present with atypical radiographic appearances such as interstitial infiltrates or lymphadenopathy, or normal chest radiographs despite bacteriologically positive disease. Extrapulmonary and disseminated tuberculosis are more common. HIV increases the clinical episodes and severity of malaria, leading to worse outcomes in pregnant women. HIV-positive people are more likely to have asymptomatic parasitemia, proportional to the degree of immunosuppression. In unstable malaria settings, HIV-positive adults are at higher risk of severe malaria and death. The clinical presentation of pneumococcal pneumonia, with fever, chest pain, and cough, is similar in HIV-positive and HIV-negative people, but HIV-positive people are more likely to have pneumococcal bacteremia and are associated with pneumococcal meningitis.
section_summaries.diagnosis: HIV infection complicates the laboratory diagnosis of tuberculosis by reducing bacillary concentration in sputum, lowering the sensitivity of bacteriologic tests like smear microscopy. Xpert MTB/RIF, an automated polymerase chain reaction-based assay, is the WHO-recommended first-line test for HIV-positive people with symptoms suggesting tuberculosis. Lateral flow assays for urinary lipoarabinomannan have sub-optimal sensitivity. Sputum culture, particularly using liquid culture media, is the most sensitive bacteriologic test, and imaging is useful. All people diagnosed with or under investigation for tuberculosis should know their HIV status. HIV-positive people entering or re-entering care should be screened for tuberculosis, including symptom screening (cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss). If bacterial pneumonia is suspected in HIV-positive people, underlying tuberculosis should be considered.
section_summaries.treatment: The treatment of tuberculosis in HIV-positive people is generally the same as for HIV-negative people, but is complicated by multiple drug-drug interactions, particularly between rifampin and protease inhibitors, non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors, and integrase inhibitors. WHO recommends standard rifampin-based anti-tuberculosis treatment along with an efavirenz-based antiretroviral regimen; dose adjustments may be needed with other regimens. Antiretroviral therapy should be initiated as soon as possible after starting anti-tuberculous treatment, except when tuberculosis involves the central nervous system. HIV infection is associated with an increased risk of malaria treatment failure. Potential interactions exist between anti-malarial and antiretroviral drugs, such as protease inhibitors increasing quinine or lumefantrine levels, and efavirenz not being co-administered with amodiaquine. In HIV-positive people on co-trimoxazole preventive therapy, sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine should not be used if malaria is diagnosed. For suspected bacterial pneumonia in HIV-positive people, empirical fluoroquinolone use should be avoided if underlying tuberculosis is a possibility.
section_summaries.prevention: Isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) is recommended to reduce the risk of tuberculosis in HIV-positive people, and effective antiretroviral therapy also reduces this risk. Measures to minimize tuberculosis transmission are essential in healthcare settings serving HIV-positive people. In malarial areas, standard anti-malarial prevention measures like insecticide-treated bed nets should be part of the care package for HIV-positive people. HIV-positive pregnant women in settings of stable malaria should receive three doses of intermittent presumptive malaria treatment during pregnancy (rather than two) if not taking co-trimoxazole preventive therapy. Co-trimoxazole preventive therapy should be continued in malaria-prevalent areas for HIV-positive individuals stable on antiretroviral therapy. Pneumococcal vaccination should be considered for HIV-positive people, especially those with CD4 counts above 200 cells/µL. Newer conjugate pneumococcal vaccines may be more efficacious, and the conjugate vaccine is effective in both HIV-positive and HIV-negative children and provides household protection for HIV-positive adults.
